summary: Gives advice on writing an RTP payload format specification, with reading tips, design practices and a template.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP carries real-time media, but each media format needs rules for packing and identifying its data. This guide helps authors make those rules work with RTP, signaling, and network conditions.

subtitle: A guide to designing an RTP packet format for carrying a particular real-time media format.

tldr.problem: A media format needs its own rules for how data fits into RTP packets and how RTP fields describe it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the RTP details, signaling, transport limits, design choices, publication process, and sections a payload-format specification should contain.
tldr.outcome: This Informational guide updates RFC 2736 and is itself updated by RFC 9751.

today: RFC 8088 is Informational, updates RFC 2736, and has been updated by RFC 9751. Its account of IETF and publication processes describes the situation when the RFC was published.

sections.title: Purpose and Preparation
sections.content:
An Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload format says how units of encoded media go into RTP packet payloads and how to use RTP header fields. Without those rules, RTP cannot carry that media format. The author needs to understand both the media coding and RTP.

The guide extends RFC 2736 with later experience, profiles, and resilience methods. It is advice rather than a protocol specification, and its descriptions of Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) processes reflect the time it was published.
sections.plainLanguage: A media format needs rules for placing its data in RTP packets. Authors need to understand both the media and the packet system before writing those rules.

sections.title: RTP Fields That Need Media-Specific Rules
sections.content:
Every payload format must define what its timestamp means and which clock rates it permits. The marker bit also needs a meaning; audio formats often use it for the start of a talk burst, while video formats often use it for the last packet of a frame.

The sequence number can help restore packet order, and the payload type identifies the format through session-specific signaling. RTP header extensions carry format-independent metadata; they must not carry information needed to decode the payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The format must explain the timestamp and marker bit. Receivers also use sequence numbers to order packets and payload types to identify their format.

sections.title: Signaling and Media Types
sections.content:
Applications use out-of-band signaling to agree on the media format and its configuration before sending media. A media type gives the format a name and can include parameters. Each specification must define how parameters work in each signaling context.

Offer/Answer parameters may be declarative, where one side states what it can receive, or negotiated, where both sides must accept the same value. The author should explain this behavior and account for path MTUs, queuing, and quality-of-service markings.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending media, programs need to agree on a format name and settings. The specification must say who chooses each setting and how the network can affect packet delivery.

sections.title: Design Choices for Payloads
sections.content:
The guide recommends keeping payload formats simple. Depending on the media, a format may combine small data units into one packet, split a large unit across packets, interleave data, or support scalable media. Each choice has trade-offs in delay, overhead, and the effect of packet loss.

The timestamp clock rate is also a design choice. Video formats have commonly used 90 kHz, while audio normally uses its sampling rate. Authors should define the rate and consider how the media behaves when packet rates are high.
sections.plainLanguage: Authors can combine small media units or split large ones, but each choice changes delay and loss behavior. The format must also define the clock used by its timestamps.

sections.title: Publication, Security, and the Template
sections.content:
A payload-format specification should describe the media, security considerations, congestion control, and IANA registrations. The security discussion should identify risks specific to the format; general RTP security mechanisms are outside it. The RFC also describes the IETF work and review process, as well as options for work in other standards bodies or proprietary formats.

Authoring tools and a complete template are provided. The template gives authors a starting structure for the media description, payload format, signaling, congestion control, IANA, and security sections.
sections.plainLanguage: A complete specification explains its media format, network behavior, security, and registrations. The RFC also provides a template to help authors organize that information.
